name: Cava
note: Spain's answer to Champagne, and by volume the biggest sparkling wine in the world. Almost entirely made in Penedès, whatever the label implies.

name: Jumilla
note: Monastrell on ungrafted vines the phylloxera louse never reached — sandy soil it can't cross.

name: Rioja
note: The one everyone's heard of. Tempranillo and American oak, the export face of Spanish wine since the 19th century.

name: Condado de Huelva
note: Once bulk wine for Jerez's blending vats, now trying to be its own thing on Zalema and Palomino.

name: Granada
note: High Alpujarra vineyards, some above 1,000m — among the highest in mainland Spain.

name: Jerez-Xérès-Sherry
note: Sherry country: Palomino grapes, flor yeast, and a fortified range from bone-dry Fino to treacle-thick Pedro Ximénez.

name: Málaga
note: Historic sweet Moscatel and PX, once shipped round the world; production is a fraction of its 19th-century peak.

name: Manzanilla-Sanlúcar de Barrameda
note: Sherry's salty cousin: same Palomino grape, aged by the Atlantic, and locals swear the sea air is the difference.

name: Montilla-Moriles
note: Sherry-style wines from Pedro Ximénez grown in such heat the grapes often need no fortifying at all.

name: Sierras de Málaga
note: The dry, still-wine label covering the same province as DO Málaga, centred on Ronda's cooler highlands.

name: Calatayud
note: Old-vine Garnacha on schist and slate, and some of Spain's best-value reds.

name: Campo de Borja
note: Garnacha country in the shadow of Moncayo — locals call it 'the empire of Garnacha'.

name: Cariñena
note: Gave its name to the grape the French call Carignan, though Garnacha now dominates the vineyards here too.

name: Somontano
note: Pyrenean foothills, and an unusually international grape list for Spain: Chardonnay and Gewürztraminer alongside the natives.

name: Urbezo
note: A small, single-producer DO carved out of Cariñena country.

name: Binissalem
note: Mallorca's oldest DO, built on the local Manto Negro grape.

name: Pla i Llevant
note: Eastern Mallorca, warmer and flatter than Binissalem, with more room for international varieties.

name: Abona
note: South Tenerife, vines up to 1,700m on volcanic ash — some of Europe's highest.

name: El Hierro
note: The smallest and westernmost Canary DO, vines trained low against the trade winds.

name: Gran Canaria
note: Terraced highland vineyards above 1,000m inside the island's volcanic caldera.

name: La Gomera
note: Tiny and little-exported; most of what's made here stays on the island.

name: La Palma
note: Ungrafted, pre-phylloxera vines on volcanic ash, some replanted after the 1971 Teneguía eruption buried the ground.

name: Lanzarote
note: Vines in individual pits scooped from black lapilli, each ringed by a stone wall against the wind. Unmistakable from the air.

name: Tacoronte-Acentejo
note: Tenerife's biggest DO by volume, mostly Listán Negro reds.

name: Valle de Güímar
note: Southeast Tenerife, a smaller neighbour to Tacoronte-Acentejo.

name: Valle de la Orotava
note: Steep terraces beneath Mount Teide, one of the oldest wine landscapes in the Canaries.

name: Ycoden-Daute-Isora
note: Northwest Tenerife; the town Icod de los Vinos rather gives away what it's known for.

name: Arlanza
note: A young DO (2007) on Ribera del Duero's northern doorstep — same Tempranillo, cooler and far less famous.

name: Arribes
note: Steep river gorges on the Portuguese border, sharing grapes with the Douro just across it.

name: Bierzo
note: Mencía from old bush vines on slate, and the region critics keep saying is 'the next big thing'.

name: Cigales
note: Historically a rosado (clarete) specialist, now making more serious reds too.

name: León
note: Prieto Picudo, a grape that barely exists outside this corner of León.

name: Ribera del Duero
note: Rioja's great rival: Tempranillo (locally Tinto Fino) grown at altitude, built for ageing, priced accordingly.

name: Rueda
note: Spain's white-wine reference: crisp, herbal Verdejo, practically the house white of Madrid.

name: Tierra del Vino de Zamora
note: Tempranillo south of Zamora city, in Ribera del Duero's shadow and considerably cheaper.

name: Toro
note: Tinta de Toro, a burlier Tempranillo strain, from some of Spain's oldest ungrafted vines.

name: Almansa
note: High-altitude Monastrell and Garnacha Tintorera on the Albacete-Alicante border.

name: Campo de Calatrava
note: One of the newest DOs (2011), carved out of the vast La Mancha plain around volcanic maars.

name: La Mancha
note: The world's largest single wine region by area — one DO covers more vineyard than most countries.

name: Manchuela
note: Bobal country: a grape long dismissed as a bulk blender, now the region's own case for itself.

name: Méntrida
note: Garnacha on Madrid's doorstep, historically the capital's everyday red.

name: Mondéjar
note: A small Guadalajara DO overshadowed by its giant neighbour, La Mancha.

name: Ribera del Júcar
note: One of the youngest DOs (2003): Bobal and Tempranillo along the Júcar river.

name: Uclés
note: Tempranillo at altitude on the Cuenca plateau, named for the hilltop monastery-village at its centre.

name: Valdepeñas
note: The historic bulk-wine engine of central Spain, now working hard to be taken seriously.

name: Alella
note: One of Spain's smallest and oldest DOs, all but swallowed by Barcelona's northern suburbs.

name: Cataluña
note: A catch-all regional DO layered over the more specific Catalan ones, mostly used for blends that cross their borders.

name: Conca de Barberà
note: Cooler and higher than neighbouring Penedès; long the source of base wine for Cava before building its own name.

name: Costers del Segre
note: A scattered DO stitched together from irrigated estates around Lleida, largely the work of one pioneering winery.

name: Empordà
note: Garnacha and Carignan on windswept Costa Brava hillsides, battered by the Tramontana wind.

name: Montsant
note: Priorat's less mythologised neighbour, wrapped around it on similar slate, at a friendlier price.

name: Penedès
note: Catalonia's biggest DO and Cava's historic engine room, now pushing still wines just as hard.

name: Pla de Bages
note: A small inland DO built around the Picapoll grape, all but unique to it.

name: Priorat
note: Steep slate (llicorella) terraces, punishingly low yields, and some of Spain's most expensive reds.

name: Tarragona
note: Coastal and workmanlike, historically supplying altar wine to half of Europe's churches.

name: Terra Alta
note: Spain's largest concentration of old-vine white Garnacha Blanca, in a hot, isolated corner near the Ebro delta.

name: Ribera del Guadiana
note: Extremadura's only DO, stitched together from five scattered subzones around the Guadiana basin.

name: Monterrei
note: Galicia's driest, hottest corner, on the Portuguese border, making fuller reds than its Atlantic-facing neighbours.

name: Rías Baixas
note: Albariño's home ground: crisp, saline whites grown on granite pergolas above the Atlantic estuaries.

name: Ribeira Sacra
note: Vines on terraces so steep they're worked by hand or winched, above the Sil and Miño canyons.

name: Ribeiro
note: Galicia's oldest wine region, exporting to England before Rioja existed as a concept.

name: Valdeorras
note: Godello country: a white grape written off as a lost cause until growers here proved otherwise.

name: Vinos de Madrid
note: Three scattered subzones around the capital; Garnacha in the west, Tempranillo and Airén elsewhere.

name: Bullas
note: Monastrell at altitude in the Sierra de Espuña foothills, Murcia's smallest DO.

name: Yecla
note: A single-town DO built almost entirely on Monastrell, much of it still dry-farmed bush vines.

name: Navarra
note: Rioja's northern neighbour, historically rosado country, now hedging across reds, whites and everything between.

name: Arabako Txakolina
note: The smallest and newest of the three Basque Txakoli DOs, scattered around the province of Álava.

name: Bizkaiko Txakolina
note: Sharp, low-alcohol Atlantic whites from Hondarribi Zuri, traditionally poured from a height to wake the fizz up.

name: Getariako Txakolina
note: The original and biggest Txakoli DO, clinging to slopes above the fishing town that gave it its name.

name: Alicante
note: Coastal Moscatel and inland Monastrell under one DO, plus Fondillón: an oxidised, barrel-aged relic few still make.

name: Utiel-Requena
note: Bobal's stronghold, once grown mostly for colour and bulk, increasingly bottled and taken seriously on its own.

name: Valencia
note: A patchwork of subzones round the city, from coastal Moscatel to the cooler Alto Turia hills inland.

name: Terras do Dão
note: Granite country ringed by mountains: Touriga Nacional reds and Encruzado whites tend to trade Douro muscle for perfume and restraint.

name: Tejo
note: The Tagus splits fertile river plains from drier limestone and sandy uplands — a former bulk-wine engine with much more range than that reputation suggests.

name: Távora-Varosa
note: Cool, high country between the Douro and Dão, best known as one of Portugal's natural homes for traditional-method sparkling wine.

name: Algarve
note: Four small southern appellations in a hot strip between mountains and sea, where vines compete with resorts for the same sunny ground.

name: Alentejo
note: Cork-oak plains and generous, ripe reds — but also the old talha tradition of fermenting wine in huge clay jars, especially around Vidigueira.

name: Beira Interior
note: Mountain-edge vineyards along Spain's border: high, dry and cold by Portuguese standards, with old vines and grapes such as Síria and Rufete.

name: Bairrada
note: Atlantic clay and limestone, formidable Baga reds, and a long sparkling-wine habit. The suckling pig pairing is practically regional law.

name: Lisboa
note: A long, windy Atlantic region containing nine DOCs — from Arinto in Bucelas to Colares vines rooted in sand behind the surf.

name: Península de Setúbal
note: Moscatel de Setúbal's fortified orange-peel richness on one side; Castelão reds from Palmela's sandy soils on the other.

name: Vinho Verde
note: Portugal's cool, rainy northwest. 'Verde' means young rather than green, and the serious Alvarinho and Loureiro bottles are neither sweet nor obligatorily fizzy.

name: Trás-os-Montes
note: The remote northeast beyond the mountains: hot summers, freezing winters, altitude and old mixed vineyards far from Portugal's export spotlight.

name: Douro
note: The same vertiginous schist terraces produce Port and increasingly serious dry wine. Demarcated in 1756, it is the historic heavyweight.
